html:
Cyrus the Great was the Persian king who founded the Achaemenid Empire, the largest the world had yet seen. He was born around 600 BCE in Persis, in south-west Iran, and died in 530 BCE.

He began as a local king under the Medes, who ruled Iran. Around 550 BCE he rebelled and took their empire. Then he turned west and east:

  • He beat King Croesus of Lydia and took Anatolia, with its Greek cities, around 546 BCE.
  • He took Babylon in 539 BCE, almost without a fight, and with it Mesopotamia and the Levant.
  • He campaigned in Central Asia, where he died in 530 BCE fighting nomads east of the Caspian.

What made him stand out was how he ruled. He kept local elites in place, honoured local gods and customs, and presented himself in each land as a lawful king. In Babylon he had the Cyrus Cylinder written, claiming that the god Marduk had chosen him and that he had let deported peoples go home.

Among those peoples were the Jews exiled in Babylon. Cyrus allowed them to return and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem, ending the Babylonian captivity. The Hebrew Bible calls him God's anointed, the only non-Jew given that title. The Greek writer Xenophon later held him up as the model of a wise ruler.

He was buried in a simple stone tomb at Pasargadae, his capital. His son Cambyses II added Egypt, and Darius the Great organised the empire that Cyrus had built.
